docs.title: Calibration
docs.text:
Experimental

Calibration tooling is experimental. The API may change in future releases.

Parameter calibration fits METANET model parameters to reference data (e.g. measured traffic data or the output of another simulator, converted to the ground-truth file format) using sliding-window nonlinear least-squares optimisation via SciPy's Trust-Region Reflective algorithm. Only METANET supports calibration; CTM has no calibratable parameters (its characteristics are entirely determined by link geometry).

For a detailed algorithmic description, see Schlapbach et al., STRC 2026.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The calibration workflow:

  1. Provide ground-truth data as a results JSON file (e.g. saved from a reference simulation with Simulation.save_results, or converted from measurements).
  2. Instantiate a Calibrator with the same Network object.
  3. Call calibrate_model_params() with the path to the saved JSON.
  4. Optionally run multi-start search (Latin Hypercube Sampling) to escape local minima, and inspect parameter correlations to detect identifiability issues.

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
from traffic_flow_models import Calibrator, METANET, METANETParams

# Initial parameter guess (the model's literature start values)
initial_params: METANETParams = {
    "tau": 18.0 / 3600,
    "nu": 60.0,
    "kappa": 40.0,
    "delta": 0.0122,
    "phi": 2.98,
    "alpha": 1.636,
}

metanet = METANET()

# Create the calibrator (takes only the network)
calibrator = Calibrator(network=net)

# Calibrate — returns (params_dict, scipy_result, param_history_array)
calibrated_params, result, param_history = calibrator.calibrate_model_params(
    # ground truth file in the results JSON format (see below)
    ground_truth_filepath="results/ground_truth/simulation_results.json",
    model=metanet,
    initial_params=initial_params,
    window_size=30,       # time steps per sliding window
    stride=15,            # step between windows (default: window_size // 2)
    model_options={"link_specific_alpha": False},
    regularization_weight=0.0,
    max_nfev=200,
    verbose=True,
    save_dir="results/calibration",
    plot_correlation="parameter_correlation.png",
    plot_param_history="param_history.png",
    correlation_title="Parameter Correlation Analysis",
)

print(calibrated_params)          # METANETParams dict with calibrated values
print(f"Cost:    {result.cost:.4e}")
print(f"Success: {result.success}")
print(f"Evals:   {result.nfev}")

The calibration targets the six METANETParams fields: tau, nu, kappa, delta, phi, and alpha. Fundamental-diagram parameters (lane_capacity, free_flow_speed, jam_density) are not calibrated — they stay on the links.

docs.title: Return values
docs.text: Value Type Description calibrated_params METANETParams Calibrated parameter dict result scipy.OptimizeResult Full optimizer state (result.cost, result.success, result.nfev, result.message) param_history NDArray[float] 2-D array (n_evals × n_params) — parameter vector at each residual evaluation

docs.title: Ground-truth file format
docs.text:
The ground truth is a JSON file with the same layout that Simulation.save_results writes and Simulation.load_results reads. Link, node, origin and destination IDs must match the Network passed to the Calibrator.

{
  "metadata": { "model_type": "METANET", "link_properties": { "...": {} } },
  "time_array": [0.0, 0.0028, 0.0056],
  "state_time_series": {
    "flows":     { "<link_id>": [[q_cell0, q_cell1], [q_cell0, q_cell1], ...] },
    "densities": { "<link_id>": [[...], ...] },
    "speeds":    { "<link_id>": [[...], ...] },
    "origin_queues": {}, "onramp_queues": {}, "offramp_queues": {}
  },
  "disturbance_time_series": {
    "origin_demands": {}, "turning_rates": {},
    "flow_boundary_conditions": {}, "density_boundary_conditions": {}
  }
}
  • time_array is in hours. State series hold one entry per time step (per-cell lists for motorway links). Disturbance series hold one entry fewer, since they apply between steps.
  • Full files (use_disturbance_from_file=True, the default) must contain all state fields (including the queue fields) and all four disturbance fields.
  • Mainline-only files (use_disturbance_from_file=False) only need flows, densities and speeds for the mainline motorway links, plus the two boundary-condition fields. Queues are optional (zero when absent); demands and turning rates are not read from the file. Instead, all four disturbance callables (origin_demands_fn, turning_rates_fn, flow_boundary_conditions_fn, density_boundary_conditions_fn) must be passed. Set metadata.model_type to "MICRO" so that Simulation.visualize and visualize_comparison also load the file in mainline-only mode.
  • Ramp metering: On-ramp controllers of the network are evaluated inside the model step on the predicted states. If a controller sets control_dt (see Ramp metering), the calibrator instead reconstructs the metering rates of all on-ramps once from the recorded states, since the model step then takes every rate as an input: rates of controllers with a control_dt are held for it, as Simulation.run does, and controllers without one are updated at every step. This needs a full file, a time step that divides control_dt, and a series that starts with a controller update (as files from Simulation.save_results do).
  • If the number of cells per link in the file differs from the network partitioning, the per-cell arrays are resampled spatially, using metadata.link_properties[<id>].cell_lengths when present (uniform cells otherwise). Use Simulation.resample_results_file to resample a file to a different time grid.

docs.title: Custom bounds
docs.text:
The default start values are the model parameters of Kotsialos, Papageorgiou, Mangeas and Haj-Salem (2002, Transportation Research Part C 10(1), 65–84, Table 1): \(\tau = 18\) s, \(\nu = 60\) km²/h, \(\kappa = 40\) veh/km/lane, \(\delta = 0.0122\), \(\varphi = 2.98\) and \(a = 1.636\). The default bounds are the METANET calibration limits of Zhao, Roncoli and Yildirimoglu (2025, Bounded-METANET, Table 1): \(a \in [0.5, 2.5]\), \(\tau \in [5, 80]\) s, \(\nu \in [10, 90]\) km²/h, \(\kappa \in [5, 50]\) veh/km/lane, \(\delta \in [10^{-4}, 4]\), with \(\varphi \in [0.01, 15]\) (no published range). The explicit relaxation term is unstable for \(\tau\) below the time step \(T\) (Zhao et al. note that the lower bound of \(\tau\) is set by the time step), so the calibrator raises a lower bound of \(\tau\) below \(T\) to \(T\) and issues a warning; this applies to the default bounds and to param_bounds. Start values and true values should lie strictly inside the bounds.

Retrieve the model's default bounds and optionally override them:

import numpy as np

lower, upper = METANET().get_calibration_bounds(network=net)

# Override specific bounds (order: tau, nu, kappa, delta, phi, alpha)
lower[0] = 20.0 / 3600  # tau ≥ 20 s
upper[1] = 60.0         # nu ≤ 60

calibrated_params, result, param_history = calibrator.calibrate_model_params(
    ground_truth_filepath="results/ground_truth/simulation_results.json",
    model=metanet,
    initial_params=initial_params,
    param_bounds=(lower, upper),
    window_size=30,
    stride=15,
    model_options={"link_specific_alpha": False},
)

docs.title: Multi-start search
docs.text:
When data are noisy or the loss surface is multimodal, use Latin Hypercube Sampling to explore the parameter space from multiple starting points. The best result across all runs is returned. Pass plot_convergence as a filename string to save a diagnostic plot of cost, evaluations, and optimality across all LHS runs:

calibrated_params, result, param_history = calibrator.calibrate_model_params(
    ground_truth_filepath="results/ground_truth/simulation_results.json",
    model=metanet,
    initial_params=initial_params,
    window_size=30,
    stride=15,
    model_options={"link_specific_alpha": False},
    regularization_weight=0.0,
    max_nfev=150,
    use_parameter_search=True,     # enable LHS multi-start
    n_samples=40,                  # number of LHS samples
    save_dir="results/calibration",
    plot_convergence="lhs_convergence.png",   # convergence across LHS runs
    plot_correlation="parameter_correlation.png",
    plot_param_history="param_history.png",
    convergence_title="Multi-Start Convergence",
    correlation_title="Parameter Correlation — LHS Best",
    verbose=True,
)

plot_convergence only produces output when use_parameter_search=True; it is silently ignored in single-start mode. Both plot_convergence and plot_correlation also accept True (uses a default filename) or False (disabled).

docs.title: Correlation analysis
docs.text:
High off-diagonal correlations (> 0.8) indicate parameter pairs that cannot be identified simultaneously. The analysis is triggered automatically during calibrate_model_params() when plot_correlation and save_dir are set. It can also be run standalone on a result returned from a previous call:

param_names = METANET().get_calibration_param_names(network=net)
# returns ['tau', 'nu', 'kappa', 'delta', 'phi', 'alpha']

calibrator.analyze_parameter_correlation(
    result=result,
    param_names=param_names,
    save_dir="results/calibration",
    filename="correlation_matrix.png",
    title="Parameter Correlation Analysis",
)

If a pair is strongly correlated, consider fixing one parameter to a physically motivated value by narrowing its bounds to a small interval around that value, then re-running.

docs.title: Regularization and noisy data
docs.text:
Each calibration window starts from the recorded state at its first time step and is predicted forward with the candidate parameters. With noisy data, this initial state is itself noisy, which biases the estimate. The calibrator therefore starts every window from a centered moving average of the recorded states, \(\hat{x}(t) = \frac{1}{|N_t|} \sum_{j \in N_t} x(j)\) with \(N_t = \{t - \tfrac{k-1}{2}, \dots, t + \tfrac{k-1}{2}\}\) restricted to the recorded time steps (initial_state_smoothing \(k\), odd, default 5; with 10 s steps about a 1-minute aggregation). The residuals still compare with the raw measurements. Use initial_state_smoothing=1 for noise-free data. The starting point is moved 0.1 % of the bound range inside the parameter bounds, because the trust region reflective method stalls when it starts on a bound.

For noisy real-world data, three further strategies improve robustness:

  1. Disable link-specific alpha (link_specific_alpha: False) to reduce the number of free parameters.
  2. Add relative Tikhonov regularization (regularization_weight \(\lambda\)) to penalize deviation from the reference parameters \(p^{\mathrm{ref}}\) (regularization_reference, default initial_params; with multi-start every run uses the same reference). The calibrator minimizes \(\lVert r(p) \rVert^2 + \lambda \sum_i \log^2(p_i / p_i^{\mathrm{ref}})\), the MAP objective of independent log-normal priors. The penalty is unit-free, so a deviation by a factor of 2 costs \(\lambda \log^2 2 \approx 0.48\,\lambda\) for every parameter (e.g. tau in hours and nu in km²/h alike). It requires positive parameters and lower bounds.
  3. Use multi-start search to avoid local minima introduced by noise.
# Experiment: noisy data with relative Tikhonov regularization (no multi-start)
calibrated_params_reg, result_reg, param_history_reg = calibrator.calibrate_model_params(
    ground_truth_filepath="results/noisy/simulation_results.json",
    model=metanet,
    initial_params=initial_params,
    window_size=30,
    stride=15,
    model_options={"link_specific_alpha": False},
    regularization_weight=0.1,     # relative (log-ratio) Tikhonov penalty
    use_parameter_search=False,
    save_dir="results/calibration",
    plot_correlation="noisy_reg_correlation.png",
    plot_param_history="noisy_reg_param_history.png",
    correlation_title="Parameter Correlation — Noisy (Regularized)",
)

docs.title: Link-specific alpha
docs.text:
Set model_options={"link_specific_alpha": True} to calibrate a separate alpha for every motorway link. The returned calibrated_params["alpha"] is then a dict[str, float] mapping link IDs to values rather than a scalar:

calibrated_params_link, result_link, param_history_link = calibrator.calibrate_model_params(
    ground_truth_filepath="results/noisy/simulation_results.json",
    model=metanet,
    initial_params=initial_params,
    window_size=30,
    stride=15,
    model_options={"link_specific_alpha": True},
    regularization_weight=0.1,
    use_parameter_search=False,
    save_dir="results/calibration",
    plot_correlation="link_alpha_correlation.png",
    plot_param_history="link_alpha_param_history.png",
    correlation_title="Parameter Correlation — Link-Specific Alpha",
)

# calibrated_params_link["alpha"] is a dict when link_specific_alpha=True
alpha = calibrated_params_link["alpha"]
if isinstance(alpha, dict):
    for link_id, alpha_val in alpha.items():
        print(f"  Link {link_id}: alpha = {alpha_val:.4f}")
else:
    print(f"  Global alpha = {alpha:.4f}")

docs.title: Comparing parameter histories
docs.text:
After running multiple experiments you can overlay their parameter trajectories to compare convergence across conditions:

param_names = ["tau", "nu", "kappa", "delta", "phi", "alpha"]

calibrator.plot_parameter_convergence(
    param_history_exact=param_history_exact,     # from exact ground truth
    param_history_noreg=param_history_noreg,     # from noisy data, no regularization
    param_history_reg=param_history_reg,         # from noisy data, with regularization
    param_names=param_names,
    true_params=true_params,                     # METANETParams ground truth (for reference lines)
    save_dir="results/calibration",
)

  • No system-level dependencies

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: This guide walks through a complete CTM simulation, introducing the main building blocks: network topology, model selection, simulation execution, and result inspection.

docs.title: 1. Build a network
docs.text:
A network consists of links connected by nodes. Virtual Origin and Destination links represent demand sources and sinks at the boundary of the modelled area.

The example below models a simple motorway stretch with a bottleneck (lane drop in the middle) and an on-ramp.

from traffic_flow_models import (
    Network, Node,
    MotorwayLink, Onramp,
    Origin, Destination,
)

# Origins (virtual demand sources)
o_main = Origin(id="o_main")
o_ramp = Origin(id="o_ramp")

# Destination (virtual sink)
dest = Destination(id="d_main")

# Links — every link needs lane_capacity, free_flow_speed, jam_density
link1  = MotorwayLink(id="m1", length=2.0, lanes=3,
                      lane_capacity=2000, free_flow_speed=100, jam_density=180)
onramp = Onramp(id="r1", length=0.5, lanes=1,
                lane_capacity=1800, free_flow_speed=80, jam_density=180)
link2  = MotorwayLink(id="m2", length=1.0, lanes=1,   # bottleneck
                      lane_capacity=2000, free_flow_speed=100, jam_density=180)
link3  = MotorwayLink(id="m3", length=1.0, lanes=3,
                      lane_capacity=2000, free_flow_speed=100, jam_density=180)

# Nodes
n0 = Node(id="n0", incoming=[o_main],          outgoing=[link1])
n1 = Node(id="n1", incoming=[link1, onramp],   outgoing=[link2])
n2 = Node(id="n2", incoming=[o_ramp],          outgoing=[onramp])
n3 = Node(id="n3", incoming=[link2],           outgoing=[link3])
n4 = Node(id="n4", incoming=[link3],           outgoing=[dest])

net = Network(nodes=[n0, n1, n2, n3, n4])

docs.title: 2. Define demand
docs.text:
Demand is a callable (t: float) -> float for each Origin, where t is the current simulation time in hours. Here we use constant or piecewise-constant demand.

main_demand = lambda t: 1500.0                              # constant 1500 veh/h
ramp_demand = lambda t: 800.0 if t < 0.5 else 400.0         # steps down after 30 min

The simulation also requires turning rates at each node (fractions of flow routed into each outgoing link) and boundary conditions at each destination:

origin_demands = {
    "o_main": main_demand,
    "o_ramp": ramp_demand,
}

turning_rates = {
    "n0": lambda t: {"m1": 1.0},
    "n1": lambda t: {"m2": 1.0},
    "n2": lambda t: {"r1": 1.0},
    "n3": lambda t: {"m3": 1.0},
    "n4": lambda t: {"d_main": 1.0},
}

destination_flow_bc    = {"d_main": lambda t: 6000.0}  # unconstrained exit
destination_density_bc = {"d_main": lambda t: 0.0}

docs.title: 3. Choose a model and run
docs.text:
CTMMETANET 
from traffic_flow_models import CTM, Simulation

# CTM takes no constructor arguments;
# fundamental-diagram parameters are set on each MotorwayLink.
sim = Simulation(network=net, model=CTM())
time_arr, states, disturbances = sim.run(
    duration=1.0,
    dt=10 / 3600,
    origin_demands=origin_demands,
    turning_rates=turning_rates,
    destination_flow_bc=destination_flow_bc,
    destination_density_bc=destination_density_bc,
    plot_results=False,
)

from traffic_flow_models import METANET, METANETParams, Simulation

# METANETParams holds the second-order coefficients only;
# fundamental-diagram parameters (vf, Qc_lane, rho_jam) stay on the links.
model_params: METANETParams = {
    "tau":   22 / 3600,  # relaxation time [h]
    "nu":    15.0,       # anticipation coefficient [km²/h]
    "kappa": 10.0,       # density smoothing [veh/km/lane]
    "delta": 1.4,        # on-ramp speed-drop coefficient
    "phi":   10.0,       # lane-drop anticipation coefficient
    "alpha": 2.0,        # FD shape exponent
}

sim = Simulation(network=net, model=METANET(), model_params=model_params)
time_arr, states, disturbances = sim.run(
    duration=1.0,
    dt=10 / 3600,
    origin_demands=origin_demands,
    turning_rates=turning_rates,
    destination_flow_bc=destination_flow_bc,
    destination_density_bc=destination_density_bc,
    plot_results=False,
)

docs.title: 4. Inspect results
docs.text:
VKT, VHT, avg_speed = sim.compute_metrics(
    states=states, dt=10 / 3600, timesteps=len(time_arr)
)
print(f"Total VKT : {VKT:.0f} veh·km")
print(f"Total VHT : {VHT:.1f} veh·h")
print(f"Mean speed: {avg_speed:.1f} km/h")

docs.title: 5. Save results and generate plots
docs.text:
Pass plot_results=True (and optionally results_dir) to run() to automatically save plots and a JSON results file:

time_arr, states, disturbances = sim.run(
    duration=1.0,
    dt=10 / 3600,
    origin_demands=origin_demands,
    turning_rates=turning_rates,
    destination_flow_bc=destination_flow_bc,
    destination_density_bc=destination_density_bc,
    plot_results=True,
    results_dir="results/quickstart",
)

To generate a basic video from saved results (every node needs a position, see Visualization):

sim.visualize(
    results_filepath="results/quickstart/simulation_results.json",
    output_filepath="results/quickstart/simulation.avi",
    fps=10,
)

Next steps:

  • Network Structure — understand the topology model in depth
  • CTM / METANET — model equations and parameter reference
  • Ramp Metering — add a controller to the simulation

docs.title: CTM vs. METANET
docs.text: Both models share the same network representation and simulation interface. The choice between them depends on the phenomena you need to capture and the availability of calibration data.

docs.title: Side-by-side comparison
docs.text: CTM METANET Order First-order Second-order State variables \(\rho, v, q\) (speed derived) \(\rho, v, q\) (speed dynamic) Fundamental diagram Triangular Exponential Parameters 3 (FD only) 9 (3 FD + 6 METANET-specific) Calibration data needed Flow + density + speed Flow + density + speed Backward wave propagation Yes Yes Capacity drop Not captured Partially captured Driver anticipation No Yes (\(\nu\), \(\kappa\) terms) On-ramp speed drop No Yes (\(\delta\) term) Lane-drop anticipation No Yes (\(\phi\) term) Hard flow upper bound Yes (always \(\leq Q_c\)) No (transient overshoots allowed) Computational cost Lower Slightly higher (extra ODE per cell)

docs.title: When to use CTM
docs.text:
• You need a fast, robust baseline with minimal parameters.
  • You are studying large-scale scenarios where the speed equation overhead matters.
  • You need a model that never violates capacity by construction.

docs.title: When to use METANET
docs.text:
• You want to capture speed dynamics: relaxation towards equilibrium, driver anticipation, and merging speed drops.
  • You are modelling scenarios where transient flow behaviour (e.g. congestion onset with capacity drop) is important.
  • You plan to use the model inside a model predictive control or gradient-based optimisation framework that benefits from smooth dynamics.

docs.title: Direct comparison
docs.text:
Because both models share the identical network topology, demands, and turning rates, running them in parallel under the same conditions requires minimal extra code:

from traffic_flow_models import CTM, METANET, METANETParams, Simulation

ctm_sim  = Simulation(network=net, model=CTM())
meta_sim = Simulation(network=net, model=METANET(), model_params=METANETParams(
    tau=22/3600, nu=15.0, kappa=10.0, delta=1.4, phi=10.0, alpha=2.0,
))

run_kwargs = dict(
    duration=1.0,
    dt=10 / 3600,
    origin_demands={"o_main": lambda t: 1500.0},
    turning_rates={
        "n_in":  lambda t: {"m1":     1.0},
        "n_out": lambda t: {"d_main": 1.0},
    },
    destination_flow_bc={"d_main": lambda t: 2000.0},
    destination_density_bc={"d_main": lambda t: 0.0},
    plot_results=False,
)
ctm_time,  ctm_states,  _ = ctm_sim.run(**run_kwargs)
meta_time, meta_states, _ = meta_sim.run(**run_kwargs)

docs.title: Cell Transmission Model (CTM)
docs.text:
CTM is a first-order macroscopic traffic flow model. It partitions motorway links into cells and advances vehicle densities in discrete time steps using a triangular fundamental diagram. Its simplicity and physical consistency make it the standard baseline for highway traffic simulation.

For full mathematical derivations, see Schlapbach et al., STRC 2026.

docs.title: Fundamental diagram
docs.text:
CTM uses a triangular fundamental diagram relating flow, density, and speed. The three parameters that fully define it are:

Parameter Symbol Unit Typical range Free-flow speed \(v_f\) km/h 80–130 Lane capacity flow \(q\_{c,\text{lane}}\) veh/h/lane 1500–2200 Jam density \(\rho\_{jam}\) veh/km/lane 100–250

The critical density (density at capacity) follows directly:

\[\rho_{cr} = \frac{Q_c^m}{\lambda \, v_f}\]

and the backward wave speed (congestion wave propagation):

\[w_m = \frac{Q_c^m}{\rho_{jam}^m - \rho_{cr}^m}\]

docs.title: Density update (first-order conservation law)
docs.text: \[ \rho_i^m(k+1) = \rho_i^m(k) + \frac{\Delta t}{L_i^m \lambda_m}   \bigl[q_{i-1}^m(k) - q_i^m(k)\bigr] \]

docs.title: Inter-cell flow (demand–supply min-rule)
docs.text:
For interior cells \(i \in \{1, \ldots, N_m - 1\}\):

\[ q_i^m(k+1) = \min\!\Bigl\{ Q_c^m,\; \underbrace{\lambda_m v_f \rho_i^m(k+1)}_{\text{demand}},\; \underbrace{w_m \bigl[\rho_{jam}^m - \rho_{i+1}^m(k+1)\bigr]}_{\text{supply}} \Bigr\} \]

The demand term limits flow in free-flow; the supply term limits it under congestion, reproducing upstream shockwave propagation.

docs.title: Speed (derived)
docs.text:
Speed is not an independent state variable in CTM — it is recovered from flow and density via the fundamental relation:

\[v_i^m(k+1) = \frac{q_i^m(k+1)}{\lambda_m \, \rho_i^m(k+1)}\]

docs.title: Node flow and proportional reduction
docs.text: At merge nodes, total incoming flow is accumulated and forwarded according to turning rates \(\beta_n^m(k)\). If the combined demand exceeds the downstream supply of any outgoing link, all incoming link flows are reduced proportionally to satisfy the constraint — a standard technique for first-order merge models. This mechanism is handled automatically by the library.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
from traffic_flow_models import CTM

# CTM has no constructor arguments.
# All fundamental-diagram parameters (free-flow speed, capacity, jam density)
# are set directly on each MotorwayLink.
ctm = CTM()

Fundamental-diagram parameters live on each link so heterogeneous networks are naturally supported:

from traffic_flow_models import MotorwayLink

# Downstream bottleneck has a lower free-flow speed
link = MotorwayLink(id="m_bottleneck", length=1.0, lanes=2,
                    lane_capacity=1800, free_flow_speed=80, jam_density=180)

docs.title: Running a CTM simulation
docs.text:
from traffic_flow_models import CTM, Simulation

sim = Simulation(network=net, model=CTM())
time_arr, states, disturbances = sim.run(
    duration=1.0,
    dt=10 / 3600,
    origin_demands={"o_main": lambda t: 1500.0},
    turning_rates={
        "n_in":  lambda t: {"m1":     1.0},
        "n_out": lambda t: {"d_main": 1.0},
    },
    destination_flow_bc={"d_main": lambda t: 2000.0},
    destination_density_bc={"d_main": lambda t: 0.0},
    plot_results=False,
)

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
CTM assumes vehicles instantaneously reach the equilibrium speed prescribed by the fundamental diagram. This means it cannot capture:

  • Capacity drop after congestion onset
  • Hysteresis in the flow–density relationship
  • Driver anticipation of downstream conditions

For these phenomena, use METANET.

docs.title: METANET
docs.text:
METANET is a second-order macroscopic traffic flow model. It supplements the first-order density conservation equation with an explicit dynamic equation for mean speed, capturing effects that CTM cannot reproduce: driver anticipation of downstream conditions, speed relaxation towards equilibrium, on-ramp merging speed drops, and lane-drop anticipation.

For full mathematical derivations, see Schlapbach et al., STRC 2026.

docs.title: Fundamental diagram
docs.text:
Unlike the triangular FD in CTM, METANET uses an exponential equilibrium speed function:

\[ V_S^m[\rho_i^m(k)] = v_f^m \exp\!\left[ -\frac{1}{\alpha_m} \left(\frac{\rho_i^m(k)}{\rho_{cr}^m}\right)^{\!\alpha_m} \right] \]

The (optionally link-specific) shape exponent \(\alpha_m\) controls how steeply speed drops with density. This provides more flexibility when fitting real-world flow–density observations compared to the triangular shape.

The critical density is defined implicitly from the capacity condition:

\[\rho_{cr}^m = \frac{Q_c^m}{\lambda_m v_f^m \exp\!\left(-\tfrac{1}{\alpha_m}\right)}\]

docs.title: Speed update equation
docs.text:
The core of METANET is a second update equation for mean speed. It has four additive components:

\[ v_i^m(k+1) = v_i^m(k) + \underbrace{\frac{\Delta t}{\tau} \Bigl[V_S^m[\rho_i^m(k)] - v_i^m(k)\Bigr]}_{\text{relaxation}} + \underbrace{\frac{\Delta t}{L_i^m} v_i^m(k) \Bigl[v_{i-1}^m(k) - v_i^m(k)\Bigr]}_{\text{convection}} \] \[ \qquad\qquad - \underbrace{\frac{\nu \Delta t}{\tau L_i^m} \frac{\rho_{i+1}^m(k) - \rho_i^m(k)}{\rho_i^m(k) + \kappa}}_{\text{anticipation}} - \underbrace{\frac{\delta \Delta t}{\lambda_1 L_1^m} \frac{q_{on}(k) \, v_1^m(k)}{\rho_1^m(k) + \kappa}}_{\text{on-ramp speed drop}} - \underbrace{\frac{\phi \Delta t}{L_{N_m}^m \lambda_m} \frac{\Delta\lambda_m \, \rho_{N_m}^m(k) \, [v_{N_m}^m(k)]^2}{\rho_{cr}^m}}_{\text{lane-drop anticipation}} \] Term Parameter Physical meaning Relaxation \(\tau\) (h) Drivers' desire to converge to equilibrium speed Convection — Speed advection along the link Anticipation \(\nu\) (km²/h), \(\kappa\) (veh/km/lane) Reaction to density gradient ahead On-ramp drop \(\delta\) Speed reduction caused by merging flow at the first cell Lane-drop \(\phi\) Speed reduction in anticipation of a downstream lane reduction

The on-ramp and lane-drop terms are non-zero only in the relevant cells; all other cells use \(q\_{on}(k)=0\) and \(\Delta\lambda_m = 0\).

Cell flow is then recovered from the fundamental relation:

\[q_i^m(k) = \lambda_m \cdot \rho_i^m(k) \cdot v_i^m(k)\]

Flows may temporarily exceed capacity

Unlike CTM, METANET does not enforce a hard upper bound on cell flow. Transient flows above \(Q_c^m\) are physically plausible and mimic real-world congestion onset dynamics such as capacity drop and hysteresis.

docs.title: Node mechanics
docs.text:
METANET requires two additional boundary quantities at link boundaries:

Virtual upstream mean speed (at the first cell of an outgoing link, merge node):

\[ v_0^m(k) = \frac{\sum_{\mu \in I_n} v_{N_\mu}^\mu(k) \cdot q_{N_\mu}^\mu(k)} {\sum_{\mu \in I_n} q_{N_\mu}^\mu(k)} \]

A flow-weighted average of the last-cell speeds of all incoming motorway links. Without upstream flow (empty or stopped links) the library uses their plain mean instead, which keeps \(v_0^m\) continuous as the flow vanishes: a stopped last cell gives 0, an empty one its free-flow speed.

Virtual downstream density (at the last cell of an incoming link, diverge node):

\[ \rho_{N_m+1}^m(k) = \frac{\sum_{\mu \in O_n} [\rho_1^\mu(k)]^2} {\sum_{\mu \in O_n} \rho_1^\mu(k)} \]

A contraharmonic mean of the first-cell densities of all outgoing motorway links (an outgoing Destination contributes its density boundary condition, off-ramps are left out). Both quantities are computed automatically by the library.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
from traffic_flow_models import METANET, METANETParams

# METANET has no constructor arguments.
# Fundamental-diagram parameters live on each MotorwayLink (lane_capacity,
# free_flow_speed, jam_density). METANETParams holds only the second-order
# coefficients that are passed to Simulation.
model_params: METANETParams = {
    "tau":   22 / 3600,  # relaxation time [h]  (~18–30 s)
    "nu":    15.0,       # anticipation coefficient [km²/h]
    "kappa": 10.0,       # density smoothing [veh/km/lane]
    "delta": 1.4,        # on-ramp speed-drop coefficient [-]
    "phi":   10.0,       # lane-drop anticipation coefficient [-]
    "alpha": 2.0,        # FD shape exponent [-]
}
metanet = METANET()

docs.title: Parameter reference
docs.text:
Parameter Symbol Unit Standard value Calibration range Effect tau \(\tau\) h 18 s (÷3600) 5–80 s (÷3600) Speed relaxation rate; larger → slower nu \(\nu\) km²/h 60 10–90 Anticipation strength; larger → stronger kappa \(\kappa\) veh/km/lane 40 5–50 Prevents division by zero in anticipation term delta \(\delta\) — 0.0122 0.0001–4 On-ramp merging speed reduction phi \(\phi\) — 2.98 0.01–15 Lane-drop anticipation magnitude alpha \(\alpha\) — 1.636 0.5–2.5 FD shape

Standard values: Kotsialos, Papageorgiou, Mangeas and Haj-Salem (2002, Transportation Research Part C 10(1), 65–84, Table 1); they are the calibration start values (METANET().get_default_calibration_params()). Calibration ranges: Zhao, Roncoli and Yildirimoglu (2025, Bounded-METANET, Table 1), except \(\varphi\), which has no published range; they are the default calibration bounds. The examples and demo scenarios use \(\tau = 22\) s, \(\nu = 15\), \(\kappa = 10\), \(\delta = 1.4\), \(\varphi = 10\), \(\alpha = 2\), which keep the flow through the demo lane drops at capacity.

Calibration sensitivity

Depending on the chosen calibration approach, different parameters may be more or less sensitive and coupled through correlation. See the Calibration guide for details.

docs.title: Running a METANET simulation
docs.text:
from traffic_flow_models import METANET, METANETParams, Simulation

model_params: METANETParams = {
    "tau": 22/3600, "nu": 15.0, "kappa": 10.0,
    "delta": 1.4, "phi": 10.0, "alpha": 2.0,
}
sim = Simulation(network=net, model=METANET(), model_params=model_params)
time_arr, states, disturbances = sim.run(
    duration=1.0,
    dt=10 / 3600,
    origin_demands={"o_main": lambda t: 1500.0},
    turning_rates={
        "n_in":  lambda t: {"m1":     1.0},
        "n_out": lambda t: {"d_main": 1.0},
    },
    destination_flow_bc={"d_main": lambda t: 2000.0},
    destination_density_bc={"d_main": lambda t: 0.0},
    plot_results=False,
)

docs.title: Performance Metrics
docs.text:
After running a simulation, call compute_metrics() to obtain standard traffic performance indicators aggregated over the entire network and simulation period.

compute_metrics() takes the raw arrays returned by run():

VKT, VHT, avg_speed = sim.compute_metrics(
    states=states,
    dt=10 / 3600,
    timesteps=len(time_arr),
)

print(f"VKT:       {VKT:.0f} veh·km")
print(f"VHT:       {VHT:.2f} veh·h")
print(f"Avg speed: {avg_speed:.1f} km/h")

docs.title: Available metrics
docs.text: Return value Unit Description VKT veh·km Total vehicle-kilometres travelled VHT veh·h Total vehicle-hours travelled (mainline + queues) avg_speed km/h Network average speed: VKT / VHT

docs.title: Excluding queue time
docs.text:
Pass ignore_queues=True to exclude time spent in origin / on-ramp / off-ramp queues from the VHT calculation (mainline only):

VKT, VHT, avg_speed = sim.compute_metrics(
    states=states,
    dt=10 / 3600,
    timesteps=len(time_arr),
    ignore_queues=True,
)

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
A Simulation binds a Network to a model:

from traffic_flow_models import Simulation, CTM

sim = Simulation(
    network=net,
    model=CTM(),
    # model_params=model_params  # required for METANET, must be None for CTM
)

Call run() to execute the time-stepping loop. All four demand/BC dicts are required and must map string IDs to callables (t: float) -> float (or, for turning rates, (t: float) -> dict[str, float]):

time_arr, states, disturbances = sim.run(
    duration=1.0,                       # total simulation time [hours]
    dt=10 / 3600,                       # time step [hours] (10 seconds)
    origin_demands={
        "o_main": lambda t: 4200.0,     # [veh/h]
        "o_ramp": lambda t: 600.0,
    },
    turning_rates={
        "n_entry": lambda t: {"m1": 1.0},
        "n_merge": lambda t: {"m2": 1.0},
        "n_split": lambda t: {"m3": 0.8, "f1": 0.2},
        "n_exit":  lambda t: {"d_main": 1.0},
        "n_ramp":  lambda t: {"r1": 1.0},
        "n_off":   lambda t: {"d_off": 1.0},
    },
    destination_flow_bc={
        "d_main": lambda t: 7000.0,     # unconstrained exit
        "d_off":  lambda t: 2000.0,
    },
    destination_density_bc={
        "d_main": lambda t: 0.0,
        "d_off":  lambda t: 0.0,
    },
    preferred_cell_size=0.5,            # target cell length [km]; default 0.5
    plot_results=False,                 # set True to auto-save plots + JSON
    results_dir="results/my_scenario",  # used when plot_results=True
    reference_results_path=None,        # optional results JSON overlaid on link plots
)

run() returns a tuple (time_array, state_history, disturbance_history):

  • time_array — 1-D NumPy array of time points [hours], length = steps + 1
  • state_history — 2-D NumPy array, shape (state_size, steps + 1)
  • disturbance_history — 2-D NumPy array, shape (disturbance_size, steps)

Cells are made longer than preferred_cell_size where needed to satisfy the CFL condition (cell length at least free_flow_speed * dt). An error is raised if a link is shorter than one such cell.

docs.title: Saving and loading results
docs.text:
Call save_results() after run() to persist results to a JSON file:

sim.save_results("results/my_scenario/results.json")

Load with the class method:

time_arr, states, disturbances, metadata = Simulation.load_results(
    filepath="results/my_scenario/results.json",
    network=net,
)

docs.title: Setting initial conditions
docs.text:
By default the network starts empty (zero density, free-flow speed). Override per link; a given initial_densities or initial_speeds dict must contain every motorway link and off-ramp:

time_arr, states, disturbances = sim.run(
    ...,
    initial_densities={"m1": 20.0, "m2": 50.0, "m3": 20.0, "f1": 0.0},  # scalar applies to all cells
    initial_speeds={"m1": 95.0, "m2": 95.0, "m3": 95.0, "f1": 80.0},
    initial_origin_queues={"o_main": 100.0},
)

docs.title: Automatic plots during run()
docs.text:
Pass plot_results=True to run() to automatically generate and save plots (density, flow, speed per link; queue plots for origins and on-ramps; node summary plots) to results_dir:

time_arr, states, disturbances = sim.run(
    ...,
    plot_results=True,
    show_plots=False,               # set True to display the network topology figure
    results_dir="results/my_run",   # directory for saved figures and JSON
)

docs.title: Manual plots
docs.text:
Generate the same plots explicitly from the arrays returned by run():

sim.plot_results(
    time_array=time_arr,
    state_history=states,
    reference_state_history=None,   # optional mainline-only reference states to overlay
    disturbance_history=disturbances,
    save_dir="results/my_run",
)

docs.title: Video export
docs.text:
visualize() generates an AVI video from a saved results JSON file (requires opencv-python). Save results first, then call:

# 1. Save results after run()
sim.save_results("results/my_run/results.json")

# 2. Generate video
sim.visualize(
    results_filepath="results/my_run/results.json",
    output_filepath="results/my_run/simulation.avi",
    fps=10,
